strengths: The paper addresses a relevant evaluation problem: how collaboration affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding. Its focus on human workflows contributes to human-in-the-loop NLP and computational social science.
Comparing three methodological families across two contrasting corpora provides useful breadth. Keeping initial partitions fixed within systems helps reduce variation from initialization.

The evaluation distinguishes consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness. The manual audit of 2,400 document–theme pairs, with double annotation, adjudication, and reported agreement, provides valuable evidence beyond automated similarity metrics.
The presentation is generally clear, with explanatory diagrams and extensive appendices. The code/data link, theme inventories, prompt templates, and hardware information support transparency.
weaknesses: The statistical evidence for the central collaboration-effect claim is insufficiently specified. Each tool–dataset condition has only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks, and comparisons reuse those codebooks. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying the observational unit or sample sizes. Treating themes or document pairs as independent experimental replicates would constitute pseudoreplication. Participant/session dependence, uncertainty, and multiple comparisons need appropriate treatment before the significance claims can be trusted.

The design limits attribution to synchronous deliberation. The asynchronous condition consists of individuals coding without consolidation, whereas synchronous sessions involve three-person teams. Consolidation is acknowledged as unstudied, but this substantially narrows the claimed comparison of collaboration modalities. Reused participants always completed asynchronous work first, introducing possible learning effects. Allocation, session duration, and person-hours are not reported sufficiently to assess these alternatives.

Experimental accounting requires clarification. The stated design entails 3 tools × 2 datasets × 2 synchronous groups × 3 coders = 36 synchronous participant slots, yet only 33 participants are reported, each supposedly participating in at most one synchronous experiment. Additionally, Tables 15–16 contain identical theme inventories for all five Climate sessions across the relational and LLM systems. This could reflect intentional reuse, but its provenance and implications for independent theme discovery are unexplained. An anonymized participant/session map and explicit reuse protocol are necessary.

The correctness evaluation is not reproducibly defined. Figure 4 labels the outcome 'F1 Score,' while Section 5.3 describes checking sampled assigned document–theme pairs without explaining recall or false-negative construction. Aggregation across themes and sessions, treatment of unassigned documents, and confidence intervals are unclear; Table 4 reports up to 16.1% unlabeled LLM outputs. The interview study also omits its sample size and analysis procedure, limiting support for the qualitative recommendations.

The proposed quality framework needs stronger construct validation. Maximum theme matching permits many-to-one alignments and is sensitive to theme granularity, which varies substantially across sessions. SBERT similarity measures semantic proximity without necessarily capturing meaningful qualitative distinctions; selecting the closest quartile using the same embedding space further favors cohesion by construction. Sensitivity analyses and expert judgments of theme quality would help establish what these metrics support beyond descriptive clustering properties.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Climate cohesion differences of 0.01 for the relational and LLM systems do not substantiate uniformly 'much more cohesive' themes. Two corpora differing simultaneously in size, genre, length, and content cannot establish independent effects of particular dataset characteristics. Likewise, one 3B model and one inference setup provide limited support for general claims about LLM cost and reliability. Corrected inference, reconciled experimental reporting, and narrower conclusions are needed before the paper meets Findings soundness and reproducibility requirements.
